title: Hall of Famer John Riggins to have No. 44 retired by Washington Commanders
content:
The Washington Commanders will retire John Riggins’ No. 44 this season, an honor that has long seemed fitting for a franchise legend and one of the NFL’s most dominant rushers.

Riggins — Washington’s all-time leader in carries (1,988), rushing yards (7,472) and rushing touchdowns (79) — will be honored during the Commanders’ Week 9 home game against the Los Angeles Rams on Nov. 8.

He will be the third Washington player in as many years to have his jersey number immortalized by the franchise, along with Darrell Green (28) and Art Monk (81), and the seventh overall. Fellow Ring of Famers Sammy Baugh (33), Bobby Mitchell (49), Sonny Jurgensen (9) and Sean Taylor (21) were previously honored.

“There are certain players whose impact goes far beyond statistics, championships and accolades,” owner Josh Harris said in a statement. “They become woven into the identity of a franchise. John Riggins is one of those players.”

A first-round pick by the New York Jets in 1971, Riggins spent his first five NFL seasons with the Jets before signing with Washington in 1976. At 6-foot-2, 230 pounds, Riggins was a true workhorse back whose relentlessness made him one of the game’s uniquely impressive rushers — a bulldozer with deceptive speed and a rebellious spirit off the field.

In his nine seasons with Washington, Riggins topped 1,000 rushing yards four times and led the NFL in rushing touchdowns twice. Including the playoffs, he had 25 100-yard rushing games for Washington.

Riggins’ most iconic performance came during the 1982 postseason, when he ran the ball 38 times for 166 yards to lead Washington to a 27-17 Super Bowl XVII win — the franchise’s first Super Bowl victory — over the Miami Dolphins. On fourth-and-inches with about 10 minutes remaining, Riggins took a handoff and powered his way upfield for a 43-yard go-ahead score. He was named Super Bowl MVP, but his remarkable performance stretched throughout that entire postseason; in four games, he amassed 610 rushing yards on 136 carries, totals that still stand as NFL postseason records.

“‘Riggo,’ as many know him, helped define one of the most successful eras in our history,” Harris added in the statement. “He played the game with a rare combination of physicality, fearlessness, and personality that captivated fans and inspired his teammates. … Our fans not only admired him, they identified with him. He is authentic, unapologetically himself and deeply connected to the people around him.”

Riggins was the rare player who performed better as he aged.

He produced more in his 30s (5,683 rushing yards, 71 rushing TDs) than in his 20s (5,669 yards, 33 TDs), an astounding feat considering he didn’t play at all in 1980; he sat out the season because of a contract dispute, then returned for Joe Gibbs’ first year as Washington’s head coach.

“I’ll start off by saying I’m bored, I’m broke and I’m back,” Riggins famously quipped to reporters at the start of training camp in ’81.

In 1983, Riggins garnered his lone first-team All-Pro honor after rushing for a career-best 1,347 yards and a then-NFL record 24 touchdowns. He added six more touchdowns in the postseason, three of which were against the Los Angeles Rams in the divisional round.

He finished his 14-year NFL career with 11,352 rushing yards and 104 rushing touchdowns, to go with 2,090 receiving yards and 12 TDs.

Riggins was inducted into Washington’s Ring of Fame in 1990 alongside former quarterback Joe Theismann. Unlike Theismann, however, who stood at midfield in a suit during the celebration, Riggins ran out of the tunnel in full uniform and pads as the crowd roared.

“I remember running out there and Theismann’s looking at me with a quizzical look on his face and he’s going, ‘John. Why?’” Riggins later recalled to NFL Films. “And I told him, I said, ‘I had to hear it just one more time.’”

Two years later, in 1992, Riggins was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame, where he memorably told the crowd that “the news of my craziness has been greatly exaggerated. … I am the brute with a woman’s soul — my mother’s.”

The Commanders’ retirement of Riggins’ jersey number, while seemingly long overdue, represents more than a storied career. It’s also a reflection of his slowly repaired relationship with the franchise after decades of turmoil under former owner Daniel Snyder. Riggins stayed away from the team for years during Snyder’s tenure and publicly denounced the former owner for his “business practices,” labeling him a “bad guy” who has “the mindset of a child” and “knows nothing about football, absolutely nothing.”

It wasn’t until Harris and his group of investors purchased the team in 2023 that Riggins finally returned to Northwest Stadium to attend a game. He has attended multiple since, as well as an OTA practice this year.

“John has meant so much to this franchise, our fans and the game of football,” Harris said. “That’s why we’re proud to retire his No. 44 on November 8 and honor a legacy that will forever be a part of our history.”
